To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the prevalence of hypertension in the general population is 20% and is higher in the elderly, 2) the prevalence of undetected hypertension is 40% and 3) 50% of those with hypertension are treated and 25% of those treated are controlled to less than 160/90.

1) the quality of care for hypertension in general practice is poor, with a large number of people with hypertension being untreated and with a substantial number of patients not receiving adequate treatment, and 2) the quality of case finding for hypertension is poor.
the quality of care in managing hypertensive patients is poor.

the extent of case finding in general practices in inner London and north west London; the proportion of patients with a raised blood-pressure at some time in their lives who are being treated; the extent of treatment of patients with raised blood-pressure at the time of examination; the extent to which patients with raised blood pressure are being treated with a diastolic blood pressure of 90 mm H or less; the extent to and type of treatment given to patients with raised blood pressures; the extent to, and
the quality of care in managing patients with hypertension.
the quality of care in managing high blood pressure in the general population.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the general practitioner is not doing a good job in the diagnosis and treatment of hypertension in his patients, and that the problem is worse in inner than outer London.

the general practitioners in the inner London area have been less effective in the detection of hypertension, in comparison with the outer London area, and that the detection of raised blood pressure in the older patients has been more successful than that in the younger age group, but that the treatment of the raised blood pressure has not been successful in the younger group.
the quality of care in managing patients with hypertension is poor, but there are no differences between training and nontraining practices.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is an urgent need for general practitioners in inner city areas to detect and treat raised blood pressure in their patients.
there is a need for general practitioners in inner London to detect and treat more hypertension and that this could be done by systematic case finding.
we need to do a lot more in the way of case finding, but that we need to improve the quality of care we offer to those with hypertension once we have found them.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can use the same methods to detect and treat patients with hypertension.
we have to be more aggressive in the treatment of hypertension.
there’s a huge need for better education and awareness about the dangers of hypertension and how to treat it.
